03 — Exploratory data analysis on the subset¶

Converted from scripts/03_eda.py (Derrick, data prep / exploration).

Reads the daily subset CSV and produces five charts (sales distribution, sales by condition, sales over time, sales by temperature, sales by stockout hours) plus summary numbers for the meeting. Charts are saved to outputs/eda/.

Run from the Data Prep - Derrick folder (after running notebook 02, which creates the CSV).

Where this fits — CRISP-DM Phase 2 -> 4 bridge: Explore, then screen features¶

The charts below are the Explore Data task of Data Understanding — univariate distributions, trends over time, and attribute interactions — now extended with a feature screen (Week 7, section 9) that gets us ready for Modeling (Phase 4).

Looking ahead to modeling (Week 8 algorithm taxonomy). Our target (sale_amount / est_demand) is numeric, so the appropriate baseline algorithms are Regression Trees (CART) and Multiple Linear Regression — the supervised numeric-target branch — not the classifiers from Weeks 12-13, which need a categorical label. This matches the proposal's plan (a previous-week baseline, linear regression, and Random Forest regression, compared with MAE / RMSE on a chronological hold-out).

Treat identifiers as categories (proposal §3)¶

The id columns (city_id, store_id, product_id, category ids) are codes, not quantities — averaging or scaling them would be meaningless — so we set them to the pandas category type before exploring further.

In [4]:
# identifiers are codes, so mark them as categorical rather than numbers
id_cols = ["city_id", "store_id", "management_group_id", "product_id",
           "first_category_id", "second_category_id", "third_category_id"]
for col in id_cols:
    df[col] = df[col].astype("category")

print("identifier columns now categorical:")

# 1) distribution of daily sales -- log-scale histogram + boxplot (raw scale hides the right skew)
fig, axes = plt.subplots(1, 2, figsize=(12, 4), gridspec_kw={'width_ratios': [3, 1]})
axes[0].hist(df['sale_amount'], bins=60, color='#4477aa', edgecolor='white')
axes[0].set_yscale('log')
axes[0].set_xlabel('daily sale_amount (normalized)'); axes[0].set_ylabel('store-product-days (log scale)')
axes[0].set_title('Distribution of daily sales (log y reveals the long tail)')
axes[1].boxplot(df['sale_amount'], widths=0.5, patch_artist=True,
                boxprops=dict(facecolor='#4477aa', alpha=0.6), medianprops=dict(color='#cc6677'))
axes[1].set_title('Spread'); axes[1].set_ylabel('sale_amount'); axes[1].set_xticks([])
plt.tight_layout(); plt.savefig('outputs/eda/01_sales_distribution.png', dpi=150); plt.show()

What we see:¶

heavily right-skewed — most days have low sales, a long tail of high-sales days.

Interpret:¶

The data is not Normal Distributed.

Conclusion:¶

  1. Plain linear regression assumptions (normal errors) may be strained. Consider log-transforming the target, or use tree-based models (which don't care about distribution shape).

  2. Many near-zero sales days likely correspond to stockout days — a clue that appears again in chart 5.

The point about promotion being correlated with discount is correct and later confirmed by the VIF/correlation analysis in section 9. In [9]:
# 5) sales vs how many hours the item was out of stock
bins, names = [-1,0,3,7,11,24], ["0","1-3","4-7","8-11","12+"]
df["so_bucket"] = pd.cut(df["stock_hour6_22_cnt"], bins=bins, labels=names)
so = df.groupby("so_bucket", observed=True)["sale_amount"].mean()
plt.figure(figsize=(7,4))
plt.bar(so.index.astype(str), so.values, color="#cc6677")
plt.xlabel("out-of-stock hours in the day"); plt.ylabel("mean observed sale_amount")
plt.title("Average observed sales by stockout hours")
plt.tight_layout(); plt.savefig("outputs/eda/05_stockout_effect.png", dpi=150);
plt.show()

What you see: Mean observed sales drop as out-of-stock hours rise (1.14 → 1.95 → 1.49 → 1.28 → 0.46).

The wrong conclusion: "Stockouts reduce sales, so we should avoid them" — technically true but misleading, because it treats correlation as the whole story.

The right conclusion (the notebook's main insight): This is censoring / MNAR. When an item is out of stock, sales can't be recorded — so sale_amount understates demand on those days. You are not seeing lower demand; you're seeing missing data. High-demand items are precisely the ones that sell out, so the "0 hours stockout" bucket is full of low-demand items

6) Demand-aware view: adjusting for stockouts¶

sale_amount only counts sales that actually happened. When an item was out of stock, no sales could be recorded, so sale_amount understates the real demand on those days. Chart 05 above shows observed sales dropping as stockout hours rise — but part of that drop is just this censoring, not customers wanting less.

Here is a simple correction. During business hours (6:00–22:00, which is 16 one-hour slots) the column stock_hour6_22_cnt tells us how many hours the item was out of stock. We assume the item would have sold at its normal in-stock rate during the hours it was unavailable, and scale the observed sales up by how much of the day it was actually available:

availability     = (16 - stockout_hours) / 16
estimated_demand = observed_sales / availability

Days where the item was out of stock for all 16 business hours give us nothing to scale from, so we leave those estimates blank.

In [11]:
# business-hour window used by stock_hour6_22_cnt: 6:00-22:00 = 16 one-hour slots
BUSINESS_HOURS = 16

# hours the item was actually on the shelf, and the share of the day it was available
df["instock_hours"] = BUSINESS_HOURS - df["stock_hour6_22_cnt"]
df["availability"] = df["instock_hours"] / BUSINESS_HOURS

# estimate the demand we would have seen if the item had been in stock all day.
# we assume the out-of-stock hours would have sold at the same rate as the in-stock
# hours, so we scale observed sales up by the availability rate. days that were out
# of stock the whole business day give us nothing to scale from, so we leave their
# estimate blank (NaN) instead of dividing by zero.
df["est_demand"] = np.nan
in_stock = df["availability"] > 0
df.loc[in_stock, "est_demand"] = df.loc[in_stock, "sale_amount"] / df.loc[in_stock, "availability"]

print("days out of stock all business hours (no estimate):", int((df["availability"] == 0).sum()))
print(f"mean observed sale_amount: {df['sale_amount'].mean():.2f}")
print(f"mean estimated demand:     {df['est_demand'].mean():.2f}")

days out of stock all business hours (no estimate): 370
mean observed sale_amount: 1.22
mean estimated demand:     1.81

What this shows¶

The combined bar chart (chart 06) and the table show observed sales falling (1.14 → 0.46) while estimated demand rises (1.14 → 4.72). The correlation flips from -0.08 to +0.25.

  • Observed sales fall as stockout hours rise, but estimated demand rises.
  • So the decline in chart 05 is mostly censoring, not weaker demand: the items that run out are the high-demand ones, and sale_amount cannot record sales once the shelf is empty.
  • Use sale_amount as observed sales and est_demand as a rough demand proxy. The proxy assumes out-of-stock hours would have sold at the same rate as in-stock hours that day — a simplification — and it says nothing about days that were out of stock the whole time (left blank).

8) Variation across stores and series¶

The proposal asks us to compare sales across the selected stores and products to find useful variation. Left: average sales per store (colored by city). Right: the spread of average sales across all 100 store-product series.

What this shows: The store bar chart shows means ranging from about 0.9 to 1.7. The ECDF shows a long right tail. This is the "useful variation" the proposal wanted to surface: store and product clearly matter, which supports keeping them as predictors and motivates grouping similar series (e.g., clustering) later.

9) Feature screening (Weeks 7 & 8)¶

Before modeling we screen the candidate predictors on two questions from the feature- selection lecture (Week 7):

  1. Relevance — how strongly does each predictor correlate with the target? (Pearson correlation, a dependence measure.)
  2. Redundancy — do predictors duplicate each other? We use the Variance Inflation Factor (VIF); the Week 8 rule of thumb flags VIF > 5 (or |r| > 0.8).
In [15]:
# --- Feature screening: relevance and redundancy (Weeks 7 & 8) ---
predictors = ["discount", "stock_hour6_22_cnt", "holiday_flag", "activity_flag",
              "precpt", "avg_temperature", "avg_humidity", "avg_wind_level"]

# 1) Relevance: correlation of each predictor with the target.
#    We show it against BOTH the observed target and the stockout-adjusted demand.
relevance = df[predictors + ["sale_amount", "est_demand"]].corr()[["sale_amount", "est_demand"]]
print("Pearson correlation with the target:")
print(relevance.loc[predictors].round(3).to_string())

# 2) Redundancy: multicollinearity among the predictors.
#    VIF_i is the i-th diagonal entry of the inverse of the predictor correlation matrix.
corr_matrix = df[predictors].corr()
vif = np.diag(np.linalg.inv(corr_matrix.values))
vif_table = pd.Series(vif, index=predictors).round(2)
print("\nVariance Inflation Factor (VIF)   [rule of thumb: watch VIF > 5]:")
print(vif_table.to_string())

# --- relevance + VIF as bars (clearer than the text tables above) ---
rel = relevance.loc[predictors, 'sale_amount'].sort_values()
fig, axes = plt.subplots(1, 2, figsize=(13, 4.5))
axes[0].barh(rel.index, rel.values, color=['#cc6677' if v < 0 else '#4477aa' for v in rel.values])
axes[0].axvline(0, color='#999999', lw=1)
axes[0].set_title('Relevance: Pearson correlation with sale_amount'); axes[0].set_xlabel('r')
vt = vif_table.sort_values()
axes[1].barh(vt.index, vt.values, color=['#cc6677' if v > 5 else '#4477aa' for v in vt.values])
axes[1].axvline(5, color='#cc6677', ls='--', lw=1, label='VIF = 5 rule')
axes[1].set_title('Redundancy: VIF (all < 3 -> no multicollinearity)'); axes[1].set_xlabel('VIF'); axes[1].legend()
plt.tight_layout(); plt.savefig('outputs/eda/10_feature_screen.png', dpi=150); plt.show()
print('saved outputs/eda/10_feature_screen.png')

Reading the screen (Weeks 6-8):

The printed correlation table shows discount -0.208, holiday_flag +0.165, stock_hour6_22_cnt -0.077 (observed) and +0.255 (demand). The VIF table shows max 2.81 for precpt. The statement about availability and stock_hour6_22_cnt having r = -1.0 is correct by construction (availability = (16 - stockout_hours)/16). The correlation between discount and activity_flag is not explicitly printed here but is consistent with the earlier observation.

  • Most relevant predictors: discount (r ~ -0.21 with sales: a lower price ratio, i.e. a deeper discount, goes with higher sales) and holiday_flag (r ~ +0.17). activity_flag and all weather variables are weak (|r| <= 0.07).
  • The censoring shows up again: stock_hour6_22_cnt correlates -0.08 with observed sales but +0.26 with estimated demand — the sign flips once we undo the stockout censoring. This is the Week 6 MNAR pattern: the "missing" demand is tied to its own size, because high-demand items are the ones that sell out.
  • Redundancy: every VIF is below 3 (highest ~2.8 for precipitation), well under the > 5 rule, so there is no multicollinearity problem among these predictors. The one exact redundancy is by construction — availability and stock_hour6_22_cnt carry identical information (r = -1.0), so a model keeps one, never both. discount and activity_flag are moderately related (r ~ -0.76, promotions usually come with price cuts) — worth watching, but under the |r| > 0.8 threshold.
  • Modeling implication (Week 8): numeric target -> Regression Trees + Multiple Linear Regression, consistent with the proposal; the Week 12-13 classifiers would only apply if we engineered a categorical label (e.g. "will this day stock out?").

10) Time-series view: trend and weekly seasonality (Weeks 3-4)¶

Weeks 3-4 decompose a time series into trend + seasonality + residual. Here we apply that to the aggregate daily-mean sales series (additive form: Y = T + S + residual), and show the day-of-week profile. This explains why lag_7 (same weekday last week) is such a strong predictor in notebook 04.

Note: 90 days can reveal a weekly cycle but not annual seasonality (proposal limitation).

In [16]:
# 10) time-series view -- day-of-week profile + stacked additive decomposition
df["dow"] = df["dt"].dt.dayofweek
dow_means = df.groupby("dow")["sale_amount"].mean()
labels = ["Mon", "Tue", "Wed", "Thu", "Fri", "Sat", "Sun"]
daily = df.groupby("dt")["sale_amount"].mean().sort_index()
trend = daily.rolling(7, center=True).mean()
detrended = daily - trend
seasonal = detrended.groupby(daily.index.dayofweek).transform("mean")
residual = daily - trend - seasonal

fig = plt.figure(figsize=(12, 8))
gsp = fig.add_gridspec(4, 2, width_ratios=[1, 2.4])
axp = fig.add_subplot(gsp[:, 0])
axp.bar(labels, dow_means.values, color=["#4477aa"] * 5 + ["#cc6677"] * 2)
axp.set_title("Mean sales by day of week"); axp.set_ylabel("mean sale_amount"); axp.tick_params(axis='x', rotation=45)
parts = [("observed", daily.values, "black"), ("trend (7-day)", trend.values, "#cc6677"),
         ("weekly seasonal", seasonal.values, "#4477aa"), ("residual", residual.values, "#999999")]
daxes = [fig.add_subplot(gsp[i, 1]) for i in range(4)]
for ax, (nm, vals, col) in zip(daxes, parts):
    ax.plot(daily.index, vals, color=col, lw=1.4)
    if nm == "residual":
        ax.axhline(0, color="#cc6677", ls="--", lw=1)
    ax.set_ylabel(nm, fontsize=9)
for ax in daxes[:-1]:
    ax.set_xticklabels([])
daxes[-1].tick_params(axis='x', rotation=30)
fig.suptitle("Additive decomposition: observed = trend + weekly seasonal + residual", y=1.0)

What you see (2×2 panel):

Mean sales by day of week: Weekdays ~1.0–1.1, weekends ~1.63–1.65 (~50% higher). Observed + 7-day trend: flat level, recurring bumps. Weekly seasonal component: the repeating sawtooth. Residual: small and centered on zero.

How to interpret: Sales decompose additively into Y = Trend + Seasonality + Residual. The weekly seasonality is strong, trend is flat, residuals are small.

Conclusion: The weekend lift is exactly the signal lag_7 (same weekday last week) captures — which is why lag_7 ranks near the top in the models. This also justifies adding lag features.

What this shows: a strong weekly seasonality - weekends (Sat/Sun) average about 1.6 vs ~1.0-1.1 on weekdays, roughly 50% higher. The trend is fairly flat over the 90 days, and the residual is small once trend and weekday pattern are removed. The weekend lift is exactly the signal lag_7 captures, which is why it ranks near the top in the models.

Pipeline: 01 inspect → 02 subset → 03 EDA → 04 modeling → 05 classification.

EDA outcome. Sales are driven mostly by recent history, with discount and holiday adding signal and weather weak; the stockout censoring is confirmed; and the features are screened (all VIF < 3). This hands off to Phase 4 modeling (notebook 04) and the Week 9 classification demo (notebook 05).
